passages.t: ‘Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy’
passages.happening:
Psalm 126 remembers a day of joy too big to believe. “A song of ascents. When the LORD restored the captives of Zion, we were like dreamers” (verse 1). “Then our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with shouts of joy” (verse 2). Even other nations noticed: “The LORD has done great things for them” (verse 2). The people agree. “The LORD has done great things for us; we are filled with joy” (verse 3).

Then the psalm turns to prayer. “Restore our captives, O LORD, like streams in the Negev” (verse 4).

And it ends with a promise from the farm. “Those who sow in tears will reap with shouts of joy” (verse 5). “He who goes out weeping, bearing a trail of seed, will surely return with shouts of joy, carrying sheaves of grain” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The book page says this psalm seems to look back on the return from exile, which began after Persia took Babylon in 539 BC. The Hebrew words for ‘restored the captives’ can also mean ‘restored the fortunes’, as of Job (Job 42:10), so some read it of another great rescue. Most read it of the return. The note on Psalm 120 explains the Songs of Ascents.

Why ask God to restore them again, if he already did? Coming home was a great gift, but it did not end their troubles. The land was poor and the people few. So the psalm holds both: thanks for what God has done, and a prayer for more.

The Negev is the dry land in the south. Its stream beds are empty most of the year. When the winter rains come they can fill almost overnight, and the desert turns green. That is the change the people ask for: water where there was only dust.

Sowing was hard. Seed grain could have been eaten, so throwing it on the ground was a costly act of hope, especially in a hungry year. A farmer might well weep as he sowed. Harvest was the time of joy.
passages.later:
Jesus told his friends on the night before he died, “You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy” (John 16:20). He also said, “Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted” (Matthew 5:4).

Paul used the same farm picture: “Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).
passages.asks:
Are you sowing in tears right now? Doing the right thing, with no joy in it, and no harvest in sight? Psalm 126 does not say the tears are wrong. It says the weeping farmer keeps sowing, and that the harvest will come.

And remember the dreamers of verse 1. If God has done great things for you before, tell them again. Old joy feeds new hope.
